utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I've two small -- two short items I'd like to deal with before we continue to hear the testimony of the witness. The first one deals with Expert Witness Stankovic. In its latest report on the Tomasica experts, the Defence announced that it would increase the scope of proposed Expert Witness Stankovic's evidence to include evidence contained in the report of the late Dusan Dunjic. The Chamber is concerned that this could further postpone Stanisic's testimony and wonders whether the parties have discussed admission of Dunjic's report pursuant to Rule 94 bis (C). Mr. Lukic. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I would -- I don't want to intrude too deeply in the details of that discussion, but I know that Mr. McCloskey spoke with the Defence at length and expressed a great deal of Prosecution flexibility and willingness to accommodate Defence submissions in relation to the report or testimony, so I thought great progress was made. There was a -- the Defence was receptive to that spirit of accommodation, but I don't know that a formal agreement was reached. I can -- I presume Mr. Lukic can explain further, or I can contact Mr. McCloskey and get back to the Court shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are we talking about an ongoing discussion or are we talking about a matter which is close to be finalised?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we are more talking about ongoing discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when do you think that discussion would reach the next stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It has to reach the next stage very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber expects to be informed about the results - of course, preferably with a constructive proposition - within a week from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I take it we'll also hear when we will receive the report of Mr. Stankovic, because it seems that it's, rather, the admission of Mr. Dunjic's report or how to receive his evidence is at the core, but it has consequences for the expert report of Mr. Stankovic as well - and that is certainly as urgent as the other matter. Then for the next matter, I'd like to briefly turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Zec, I think you are -- our records tell us that you have used 46 minutes until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Also maybe I can inform you that we have uploaded the excerpts of Milan Martic interview that I used yesterday. It is now 65 ter 6754a and number reserved for this excerpt is P7638. Now I believe it can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe we should wait until the end of re-direct. We'll be using the same document, so maybe we will be -- we will ask to -- some additional parts to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for a moment, but at least the portions selected by the Prosecution is now in e-court. Good morning, Mr. Strbac. Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I further would like to remind you very much to focus on the questions when answering them, and Mr. Zec will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Strbac. I'm going to talk to you about one more operation conducted by the JNA and Benkovac Territorial Defence. Skabrnja and Nadin are two villages in the area between Benkovac and Zadar; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Skabrnja belongs to the Zadar municipality and Nadin to the Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: These villages were almost 99 per cent Croat villages; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You were aware that the Benkovac TO participated in the attack on Skabrnja and Nadin on 18 November 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's fine. And we will -- I'll ask a little bit more. Now this Chamber has received -- before I go on, you confirm that the unit did participant in this attack; that's right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have said that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Chamber has received General Mladic's notebooks which show that on 17 November 1991, General Mladic and the command of the 9th Corps provided tasks to the units to mop up Skabrnja and Nadin. This is in P349, page 348 through 356. And you were aware that the 9th JNA Corps led this operation; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: During the course of this operation on 18 November 1991 and thereafter, the Serb forces killed Croat civilians in these villages; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite a number of civilians lost their lives, but soldiers as well and on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You turned over to the Croatian side some -- at least 48 bodies of the victims; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33427.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is an excerpt -- actually this is an excerpt from Croatian Medical Journal from 1992. It is only in English but I will read a bit from the first paragraph. In the middle it says: "44 were killed in Skabrnja and 7 in Nadin. The age of the victims ranged from 23 to 92, almost half of them were females. Most of the victims were executed by close-range gun-shots ... several were tortured before ... one female was shot and run over by a tank." So these were the bodies that you turned over to Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so. But how they were killed and whether they had been tortured before being killed, this is something I don't know. It says here that they were, but was it really so? I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I would tender this into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33427 receives Exhibit Number P7644.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Apart from this example, Mr. Strbac, you knew that young Serb soldiers involved in these operations in 1991 were given instructions by their superiors, based on which they would cross onto the other side and kill everyone -- whoever they found; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have to say that I do not really understand what you meant by this. Onto which other side?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I was referring to the other side, Croatian side, to the front line and go to areas held by Croats, and that's where these soldiers, young Serb soldiers, would cross this line and kill whoever they found; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. This is the first time I hear that, from you. There was the action that you talked about, Skabrnja and Nadin, where a two-day battle was fought; it was very fierce and there were dead on both sides. But as for the rest, if this is what you had in mind ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Zec please be asked to speak up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, you're invited to speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You testified in Hadzic case; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And it is your position that you told the truth to the Chamber in that case; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I should have said it, and I believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And what I just told you about these instructions to soldiers, based on which they would cross and kill whoever they found, is exactly what you told to the Chamber in Hadzic case. If you would like to see it, I can show it you, but this is your evidence; do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that, man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, we can call 65 ter 33410 and we would need page 115, and this is transcript from Hadzic case and we will be looking at transcript page 12550.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And here you were asked by Defence counsel about a case that you were involved in and your answer was: "If I remember this case correctly, this young soldier was brought to the front line, and his superiors told him, Everything that is on the other side is your enemy. This soldier crossed the front line himself and whoever he found there, this elderly married couple, he killed them." A few lines below you say: "Through my appeal, I defended all these young people who were forced to shoot and kill somewhere. I wanted then, and that is my wish to this day, that those who forced them to wage war on kill be brought before courts ..." So this is your evidence in Hadzic case. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but this is different from the question, that he was told to kill everybody. Here we see that he was told that everybody is enemy on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it also includes that they were forced to kill them. It's not literally the same. Mr. Zec has now read you to the literal wording of what was recorded as your testimony. Do you stand by that or do you challenge that these were your words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in a case where I defended a man who was accused the killing two elderly people who were on the other side of the front, and he was sentenced; but it cannot be generalised. As his defence attorney, I used this and my appeal, which I wrote against the sentencing judgement against him, was read out to me. So I asked that he be pardoned because he wasn't guilty. Somebody brought him to the front line and told him, This is the front line and the enemies are on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simple question is: Do you stand by your testimony you gave in the Hadzic case? That's one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no such simple answer to this, because the Prosecutor asked me a question and now this should be a general position. And it's not like that. It cannot be answered that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you a very simple question: Do you stand about what you said there? Forget about what Mr. Zec asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with the explanation that I was explaining: My appeal in a specific case in which I was the defence attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I would offer this page into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P7645, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would probably ask more pages for the context since Mr. Strbac explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then later the -- Madam Registrar will be instructed to upload new versions, if there's an extension. Witness, you said it was all about this one case, but it was also read to you: "I defended all of these young people who were forced to shoot and kill somewhere." So that it was just one individual is -- well, not fully inconsistent with your reference to "these young people who were forced to shoot and kill somewhere." Any comment to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. If they shot and there was shooting all around -- at one point I defended 30 murders, some killed their own fathers, some killed their fellow fighters, and so on. So whoever was accused as a lawyer, I defended them, and that was the sense in which I said that. So I condemned war, as such, at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was your case that they were forced to kill their own fathers, that they were forced to kill their fellow fighters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could not be said that they were forced. No one put a gun to their forehead and said, Shoot at your father. It was a war situation. So when you have such a situation and there are weapons all around, it's easy to pull the trigger and kill even your closest ones, let alone the enemies; so that was philosophical view on war, which has nothing to do with what the Prosecutor is asking me right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would have any specific examples of cases where you defended a soldier who was forced - by whatever means - to kill either his father or his fellow fighter, I'd like to hear what the name of that case is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, nor did I defend a man who was forced by anyone to shoot anyone. The man I defended I think his name was Nikola Gagic, it was a young man --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question and you're telling me that you could not provide me with such a case. Mr. Zec, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It simply wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, listen to the next question and answer it, please. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Following the events in Skabrnja and Nadin, the remaining women, children, elderly were put on buses, transported to Benkovac; and then within a day or two you returned them to the Croat side as well. Right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yesterday when you said -- when Mr. Lukic asked you whether Serbs offered Croat civilians in exchanges, you said that both sides held some civilians. This is transcript page 41100. And you also provided an example when your people in Benkovac arrested eight Croats to be exchanged for Serbs. This is in transcript page 41081. Now, through this process of exchanges, these civilians were taken out of the territory of the SAO Krajina to the other side, to the Croat-held territory; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to clarify that to me. Make the question a bit clearer. You asked me about what I did with regard to the civilians in Skabrnja and then you continued with something else. Can you please clarify the question? Does it have to do with the Skabrnja/Nadin incident or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Skabrnja/Nadin you confirmed that you -- that these people transferred to the other side, to the Croat side. Now I was asking you about your evidence from yesterday, when you were talking about civilians -- that parties to the conflict had civilians detained, and then you provided an example when your people in Benkovac arrested Croat civilians for exchanges. And my simple question is like: All these civilians were arrested, they were taken out of the territory of SAO Krajina to the other side, to the Croat side; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which "all civilians"? Do you mean the ones who were arrested in Benkovac, the eight of them, or from Skabrnja or from Nadin? Who is "everyone"? Who are all these civilians, which "all"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's take this example of these eight Croats in Benkovac. They were arrested, they were taken out of SAO Krajina, and they were transferred to the Croat-held territory?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I think you said "yes," but it didn't make it into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You confirmed that they were transferred to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I exchanged them. I talked about that yesterday. That was my first exchange. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33419, and this is an article from Slobodna Dalmacija from August 1991. It is about an exchange near Skabrnja between Croat and Serb side. In the B/C/S if we can focus to the last column, to the right; and English, it's in the first page of this partial translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So just below the title, the last paragraph, it says: "At that moment, the Benkovac lawyer Savo Strbac arrived and signed the exchange documents on behalf of the Benkovac side." A few lines below there is a reference to eight Croats who were exchanged. So this is the exchange that you were talking about, about the eight Croats, your first exchange; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was the exchange. As to whether this is correct as we see it written, that's a different discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, in that same paragraph, a little bit further it says -- there is a question: "Why were all these men detained for three days? One said: "'I deliver newspapers to Vjesnik newsstands in Benkovac, and there in front of one newsstand they just picked me up ... it seemed to me that Martic's men could have picked up anyone else in the same way,' says Brato Vulelija, 'indeed they picked up the barber from his shop and most of the others from a bus ..." So this is how these people were arrested; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. And I said that before and I repeat: Five Serbs were arrested on the Croatian side; and then in Benkovac, eight men were arrested, and that was the exchange. And I wrote a story about it during the war; it was published, printed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think yesterday you didn't explain for what reasons they were arrested. You said they were arrested, they were exchanged. Were they arrested in order to be exchanged, or were there other reasons to arrest them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This group was arrested only for the exchange. Those people who went to have a swim in the sea were arrested just for the purpose of being exchanged. At that time, it was like you return your people -- our people to us and we'll return yours. That's how it happened in those times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: However wrong that may be to arrest people while swimming in the sea, what's the legal justification for then arresting eight Croats if it is only for the purposes of an exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever the police wrote down, I couldn't see it. I was just told about this because I was going to Zadar to attend a hearing for those five. They told me, Just tell them if they release our people, we'll release theirs. I don't know if they had any legal basis or those men were just brought to the police station and awaited the result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking about the arrest of the eight Croats, not the Serbs that were arrested but the Croats, what the legal basis for their arrest was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about them. I could see the list, the paper for Serbs but not for the Croats. Whether there was any legal basis or not, I don't know. What I was saying a moment ago, I was talking about them. They were just brought to the police station and they told me they had stayed there for two or three days, awaiting the outcome, awaiting the exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood your testimony of yesterday - but please correct me when I'm wrong - that five Serbs were arrested for no good reasons and that then eight Croats were arrested in order to arrange an exchange. And what I'm asking you is the reasons why those eight Croats were arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just said what I was telling yesterday. I understood they were arrested only for the purpose of being exchanged for those five. There is no big philosophy there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there we are talking about the same. Now, what is the legal basis for arresting eight Croats -- is there any basis in law to be find to arrest eight Croats in order to exchange them against five Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going in circles. I'm telling, I didn't see anything in writing. I only know what the police told me; namely, that they were available for an exchange. I can go on repeating this until tomorrow. If you ask me personally, my opinion was that there was no legal basis. They were just brought there. They were normal people. They were going about their business. Their only fault was that they were Croats, just like the fault of the others was only that they were Serbs, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That clarifies the matter. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I would tender this article into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33419 receives Exhibit Number P7646, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed. Mr. Lukic, I take it that if the context, the remainder of the article, is relevant, that you'll add portions to the small portion that was translated for us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we see now 65 ter 33428.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is an article from Agence Press France and we have it only in English, but I will read what it says at the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If we can turn to second page. Around the middle it says: "'We have no choice,' insisted Savo Strbac, government secretary in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. 'It is out of the question for us to return to Croatia. Our final goal is union with other Serbs (in Bosnia and the Republic of Serbia).'" So, Mr. Strbac, this was the position of your government; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was elected secretary of the government towards the end of April 1993 - it's no secret - and I remained in that position as long as the RSK lasted; that is to say, until 4 August 1995. But in addition to that, I was also president of the commission for prisoner exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And my question was: This quote of yours that I just read to you, that -- and if you want I can read again. For example, it says: "It's out of question for us to return to Croatia. Our final goal is union with other Serbs (in Bosnia and the Republic of Serbia)." This was the position of your government where you served; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are taking out of the context of a whole text one sentence which I'm supposed to confirm. It's very different than it sounds when you take one sentence out of its context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this is your statement, do you dispute that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I said something similar, but I was never given these texts to revise them or authorise them before publishing. It's very difficult to control what was published in the foreign press. I could tell you what my real positions were, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I would tender this article into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33428 receives Exhibit Number P7647, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have time. I don't know what kind of exercise is -- what's this? Can we cross-examine the journalist? I don't know. We don't know what's this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac could not even see the text, it's in English, so we -- this cannot be presented to the witness in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it has been presented to him as something that was published and whether he stands by -- whether he said -- spoke those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He said: No, I don't remember, maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's his evidence. So then we know that what is written here, that the witness says that he may have said something similar but that he has not had an opportunity -- that's the evidence so that we are able to evaluate and not just look at this but understand it in the context of what the witness told us about it. And that makes it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still, I don't like the Chamber to be poisoned by this kind of evidence and this kind of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether we are poisoned or not or whether it gives us an opportunity to, for example, to say we cannot rely -- I'm not saying that we do, but that we have a possibility to say this was published, it was put to the witness, this was his evidence about it. And then if there's any poison, then at least it's a detox exercise which is, to some extent, done by the Prosecution. But the number P7647 you rightly, by the way, Mr. Lukic, you intervened before I gave the decision on admission. P7647 is admitted. Then -- but that's another matter. Mr. Zec, we admitted into evidence and left it open whether it should perhaps -- whether other pages should be extended, but P7645, which is 65 ter 33410, I think you used one page and you said you'd like to have that page in evidence but the document contains 119 pages as uploaded into e-court. So if you would take care that we get the final excerpt which we need and which you apparently were seeking to tender. Meanwhile --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We can look into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you certainly should do that. Meanwhile, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have now 65 ter 33249.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Strbac, this is a press report of Slobodan Milosevic's speech from 1992. If you look in the third paragraph, which starts with: "The Republic of Serbia helped the Serbian people ..." And if you look over, it refers - among other things - to arming and sending volunteers to Croatia. And now we talk -- you talked yesterday about Croats arming themselves, but you also knew that Serbs in Croatia were also arming in co-operation with the authorities of the Republic of Serbia, just like Mr. President says here; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you tell me, what is the question? Am I supposed to confirm what is written in this text or to tell you what I know about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: When you read the paragraph and it refers to help from Serbia includes arming and sending volunteers to Croatia, you were also aware of this sort of co-operation between the authorities in SAO Krajina with the authorities of the Republic of Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was co-operation. I can't even see it written here as you interpreted it. All you took out of all this is assistance in arms. I see arms primarily through a firm commitment of Serbia towards the people and the army. Where did you find what you are putting to me? There is mention of assistance in funds, clothing, food, et cetera. Where did you see that weapons were being sent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you read that whole paragraph, to start with, Mr. Strbac. Then if you find it, then we can proceed; if you still do not find it, Mr. Zec will read it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found it. There is one word where it says "in weapons too."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: At the end of the paragraph -- at the end of the paragraph also it refers to volunteers to Croatia. Now you know about this sort of co-operation; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you want me to tell you now, whether there were volunteers from Serbia in Croatia? Yes, there were. Throughout the war, people were coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And with weapons as well; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I supposes so. It says "in arms too." What that mean, I don't know. Maybe you know what is meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we see 65 ter 7456.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know where you're heading, Mr. Zec, but at a certain moment, I think the details may not be of such importance that we should look at every interview given. Apart from that, of course, interviews in the way they are presented in newspapers is always a bit problematic anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'll -- perhaps just one more document just to show that -- this witness was in position also to know about these activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then if you say just this document, then let's look at that time. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we see 65 ter 07468.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will not look at this one? The one on our screen - which is it? - 7456?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's fine. We can go -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We go to the next one. We now look at 65 ter 7468.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Strbac, this is a mobilisation order by Milan Babic for the SAO Krajina TO and requests from Serbia to get support from MUP Serbia. So we see that published -- request is directed to MUP of Serbia. This is a reflection that the SAO Krajina authorities knew that they could get assistance from Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know what to tell you. Everything is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, you were man who was collecting information about the events in the former Yugoslavia. You -- you -- you were chief of intelligence of the Benkovac TO at the time, and this is mobilisation order for the TOs. You must have known that this is what was taking place at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. Why would I have to know about this option? I became secretary of the government in April two years later. Why would I have to know about each order?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is the time when you were chief of intelligence in the TO Benkovac, and this is order to the -- to form TO -- mobilised TO units in Krajina. Are you saying that somehow this -- this -- this information didn't get to you somehow?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I've never seen this order before now, but even without the document, you know that mobilisation was going on. I told you how I myself was mobilised in October 1991 in the command of the Knin Corps, and from 1977 I was member of the Territorial Defence of the Benkovac municipality staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Zec suggested to you - because there's both mobilisation of the TO and a request for assistance by the Republic of Serbia - he suggested to you that you should have known about it. You've said -- told us that you have never seen this. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I would tender these two documents, and I complete my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you'd tendered two documents. I think we had --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I can read the 65 ter's. First is 65 ter 33249.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was what exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is the speech of Slobodan Milosevic from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It wasn't used in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there was an interview -- yes, I'm just wondering. Let me see. Isn't that the one where we -- where I asked you whether you want to further deal with it and you said: No, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The one that I skipped is 65 ter 7456.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Registrar, for the remaining two documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33249 receives Exhibit Number P7648. 65 ter number 07468 receives Exhibit Number P7649, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7648 and P7469 are admitted into -- sorry, I misspoke. P7648 and P --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really have -- where -- can we be directed in the transcript where 7456 was used, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I'm really confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 7546 [sic] is not being tendered Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh. I apologise. I'm a bit lost in these numbers, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I was misquoting. Now I'll try to once and forever put an end to this confusion. P7648 and P7649 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Moloto would have a question for you, Mr. Strbac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the exhibit has been removed from the screen. Mr. Strbac, you said you -- you hadn't seen this exhibit that was shown to you; therefore, you are not aware of this request. However, the question that had been put to you - and I'm going to read it to you - was slightly different from the answer you are giving. Mr. Zec said to you: "This kind of request is a reflection that the SAO Krajina authorities knew that they could get assistance from Serbia." Therefore, the question is not whether you saw this document but whether -- are you aware of the reflection or of the fact that the SAO Krajina expected to get assistance from the Serb authorities? Were you -- independently of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such questions are really difficult to answer. I can tell you whatever I want, that I did and that I didn't; it's the same. This request was obviously sent out. Now whether this request was granted, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is not about this request. That's what I have been trying to explain. Were you aware at the time that the SAO Krajina authorities expected assistance from the Serb authorities in Serbia? Just forget about this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What would it mean to you if I said either "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you don't have do ask me any questions. You are here to answer questions not to ask them. I'm just asking you to answer my question: Were you aware that the SAO Krajina authorities expected to receive assistance from Serbia? You can say I don't -- I wasn't aware; you can say, yes I was aware; or no, I wasn't aware.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll choose a fourth option. If they were asking in the first place, it means that they were expecting it. Now how much they got, I don't know; and I don't like being taught what kind of answers I'm allowed to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I also don't want to be taught what kind of questions I must ask. I have not asked whether they did request it. They did request it, that's the evidence. All I'm asking you: Were you aware of this practice of assistance by the Serb authorities to the SAO Krajina authorities? Yes, I was aware; no, I was not aware. It's a very simple question, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of my professors used to say: One doesn't fail by giving wrong answers but by asking wrong questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- we're not going to talk about professors right now, and I'm happy to accept that you don't want to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And at the same time telling us what your professors told you is an implicit criticism on my colleague Judge Moloto, which is inappropriate for a witness to make in this courtroom. Mr. Lukic, do you have -- Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, you asked me one question about 65 ter 33410. I can provide you answer now or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's wait for a second. Let's first see, because Mr. Lukic announced that -- at least I left it open that other portions would be selected as well. I know a portion had been selected at all. Mr. Lukic, any further questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do have further questions for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, it is 10.30. Perhaps it's better to start your re-examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, you may follow the usher. We'll take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, you'll now be re- examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We can keep this document on our screens. I can start with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Strbac.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have seen this document dated 1st April 1991. Was there still a joint state of Yugoslavia which included both Croatia and Serbia at the time?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, yes, it was the time when everything still existed up until January 1992, when Croatia was recognised by the international community; so there was still a joint state at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that you still have not answered or something remains unanswered. Let me just read it out to you. You did not answer Judge Moloto on page 25. Just a second, please. Page 25, line 4. I will read it in English so that you would hear again what His Honour Judge Moloto asked you and then I will ask you my question. [In English] I quote: "I have not asked whether they did request it. They did request it, that's the evidence. All I'm asking is: Were you aware of this practice of assistance by the Serb authorities to the SAO Krajina authorities? Yes, I was aware; no, I was not aware. It's a very simple question, sir." [Interpretation] So, Mr. Strbac, in April 1991, did you know that the Krajina SUP asked the Serbian SUP for assistance, did anyone inform you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one informed me about this. Whether I had heard anything or guessed, that's a different story. No one informed me about that. As I said, we still had our joint state, the SFRY, we had the JNA. It was in May 1991 only that the JNA began playing the role of the buffer zone that we discussed yesterday, and so on. So why I would have to know this? So I've already provided an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. These are actually two decisions, one is an order and the other one is the conclusion. In the order no assistance is requested, so no assistance for the TO. It is only in the conclusion that assistance from the SUP of the Republic of Serbia is requested. This conclusion adopted by the president of the Executive Board, Dr. Milan Babic, was it compulsory for the MUP at the time and for the SUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To the best of my knowledge and recollection, I don't think that this obliged anyone to do anything because, let me repeat, the joint state - the SFRY - was still in existence and it had its own armed forces. And one of the competences of the armed forces in addition to the JNA and its active-duty personnel was also the Territorial Defence, and it was well-known who could carry out mobilisation. There were laws, there were federal laws, republican laws that regulated this. There were still no new laws in existence, so this is to the best of my knowledge and recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, are you half on your feet, half not. I don't hear anything, but you switch on your microphone. What's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I apologise. The question went from specific and then became general. The thing is that he was asked specifically about this order, and the witness is repeatedly saying: I don't know, I don't know, never seen. So I let it go, so we have the answer. So that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was general whether this kind of conclusion was binding for SUP or police in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec left it as it is in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one thing, however. In the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was the position of the SAO Krajina, was that regulated in the constitution? Was that a constitutional body which was enacted in the -- in the federal constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, neither SAO Krajina nor the Republic of Serbian Krajina, they were not states or entities that were recognised even by the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, these were turbulent times. You told us yesterday that arming of the Croatian people, contrary to the constitution, was also going on at the time. But let me ask you, if you know, whether this decision on mobilisation was in accordance with the law or was it Dr. Babic's body that adopted it, contrary to the laws and against the bodies that were invested with the power of carrying out mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just answered that the Territorial Defence in SFRY and in what was still the Republic of Croatia was the component of the armed forces. There were two such components, and it was actually known who could carry out mobilisation. This was the SAO Krajina. The Serbs, after a referendum which they organised themselves, formed the SAO Krajina. There were other two Serbian Autonomous Districts later on, the Western and Eastern Slavonias; and it was only on the 19th of December - that is to say in late 1991 - that they joined to form the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And when they united, they were not recognised by anyone; and let me repeat, even Serbia never recognised it. I was the secretary of a country that was internationally unrecognised, but it was a legal subject because it was a topic of discussion at the United Nations and in many other places and I sometimes participated in these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now return to the beginning of the cross-examination and remind you, you were asked about the moment when the JNA moved from the force that acted as a buffer zone between the Croatian and the Serbian sides, which were both armed, and it was suggested to that you it happened when General Mladic arrived in Knin. You were shown a document, showing that he got there in June, and you said that the change in the way the JNA acted occurred on the 15th of September. What was it that started on 15th of September in 1991 with regard to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By order of the Croatian authorities, a general blockade of all JNA facilities began in the worst possible manner, and it was only logical, I guess, that -- or only natural that the JNA defended itself; and it was then a natural ally of the Serbs because the Serbs were also threatened by the very same authorities which had previously thrown them out of the constitution as a constituent people, as I explained yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please look at P7638.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is an interview with Milan Martic from the 14th of October, 1994. We shall see it on our screens in a second. You were shown page 10 in both versions, so that's the page we need once again. And it was suggested to you that the JNA changed its role on the basis of this because Milan Martic said that: "General Mladic came in June or July 1991, managed to create self-confidence to Serbs and openly stated that the Serbs were right?" On the following page in both languages - we need the last paragraph in both languages - Mr. Babic talks about Kijevo -- excuse me, Mr. Martic is talking about Kijevo. It is said that decision was made to attack Kijevo. We talked about how the road leading there was blocked. We talked about it yesterday. And the last sentence here reads: "We conquered Kijevo and even managed to liberate Milan Babic's village of Vrlika, Cetina, and Civljane in that area. There were no victims apart from the civilians killed by the Croatian police in withdrawal." So would you agree that there were no casualties on the Croatian side on this occasion? What do you know about this event?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't agree because I think that there were several casualties - I don't know how many - and these interviews had another role, not just to say the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know about the Serbian civilians who were killed by the Croatian police during its withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it happened, there may have been one casualty, but I don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I tried to put a question to the witness. That question which I had on my mind was: Do you know whether the victims reported here as being killed by the Croatian police in withdrawal, whether they were Serb or Croat? In your question, you said - and that's leading - "Serb civilians." I wished I would have put that question to the witness, but the answer now is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My mistake --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- makes everything clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I stand corrected. I misread -- actually, I misunderstood. You are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can I consult with Mr. Mladic just for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your voice becomes louder and louder, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here on page 7 of the same document, the penultimate paragraph. The interview is strange - one cannot see the questions here but only the answers - and we can see in the middle of the page in the English version and the penultimate paragraph in the B/C/S version reads: "There were two waves by land as well; one coming from the direction of Sibenik and Drnis, and the other one from Sinj. The police in those places got orders to take arms and liberate Knin by force, from what they called [the] 'rebel police'."? Do you have any information about plans that were made, as we see here, and that there were two waves coming from Sibenik and Drnis and Sinj towards Knin?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that this is about the 17th of August, 1990, when the Croatian police started in armoured vehicles, at first, to disarm the police forces in the Serbian municipalities; and when they were stopped by the barricades, then the Croatian side sent the police in two helicopters. And then the JNA sent two MiGs and sent back these two helicopters. But it all has to do with the 17th of August, 1990, when officially the so-called Log Revolution started -- certainly on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's see the paragraph that's above that one. It mentions the helicopters from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the question -- in Serbian that's the question. It says: "Regarding the stopping of the helicopters from Zagreb." I'm not sure if that's present in the English version, but it's there in the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but these are all answers, the text. It just says "question" and then an answer follows, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And apart from that, as far as I remember, there were attempts, several other attempts, to disarm the Serbs and to take over these territories. And there were some names, I remember an operation that was called Raseljke where some members of the Croatian army infiltrated. They were mostly disguised as civilians, but all these operations fell through because if they had succeeded, then Krajina would have fallen much earlier, it wouldn't have waited until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we shall look at P04909. It is a document from the command of the 9th Corps dated the 16th of September, 1991, so a day after the general attack on the barracks in Croatia. You were shown paragraph 2 from this document, from which we can see that in his decision General Mladic decided that in a co-ordinated action with the Knin, Benkovac, and Obrovac Territorial Defence forces, he would launch a general attack towards the sea; however, further down in the paragraph we see that he says: "Unblock the surrounded -- the encircled and cut-off JNA forces in Sinj and the -- Drnis." And in paragraph 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you look at the transcript -- oh, okay it has been corrected. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in paragraph 1, we read: "Crush the forces of the ZNG and the MUP on their marching axes and protect and break the blockade of the units, installations, warehouses, and institutions of the JNA." What does "ZNG" mean?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the name of the Croatian Home Guards. That is the name the Croats gave to their army, the National Guards Corps. I believe in September 1991, it was not officially the HVO; it will become HVO later in November of that year when the official Croatian army was proclaimed. Until then, it was the National Home Guards. That was the tactics the Croats used to make official the party troops. They legalised all those to whom they distributed weapons, and they converted them into members of the MUP. That was a big force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, who was the president of the Presidency, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean Stipe Mesic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Stipe Mesic, the Croat delegated by Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As president of the Presidency, was he the superior of Colonel Mladic? He was a colonel at that time.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Presidency of the SFRY is also the Supreme Commander of all the armed forces, according to all the legislation governing armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at P04166, please. [In English] Can we see page 42, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it was in closed session, then we should go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We should remove this document from the screen probably.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's removed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next document we need on our screens is P04913, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was shown to you yesterday, Mr. Strbac. We'll see it in a minute. It is from the Zagreb newspaper Vjesnik. It's one story from that newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S, we need page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the middle of the page, look for the word "Mladic." And the title is: "Drnis will be called Ratkovo." These words are ascribed to General Mladic. The first sentence reads: "General Ratko Mladic, the commander-in-chief of the notorious 9th Knin Corps ..." First of all, I would like to ask you: Did you know at the time whether the Zagreb newspaper Vjesnik was reporting objectively about the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I had occasion to see, and I tried to follow all the press, it did not; it was not among the more objective media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Further below, it says - sixth line approximately - fifth line in English: "Of course, journalists were once again not allowed to follow the negotiations ..." And a few lines further on, we read: "Mladic, according to the participants in the negotiations ..." Obviously this reporter signed underneath, did not hear what Mladic had said.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard that Mladic had stated Drnis would be called Ratkovo?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this article before, and the last sentence strikes me; namely, that he allegedly said Drnis would be called Ratkovo, or perhaps Mladenovo, both names derived from his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question, whether you ever heard that Mladic had stated such a thing? Because you now commented on what you read. Did you ever hear about that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I did say that. I repeat, no, this is the first time I'm reading it, in this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and the question was whether you ever heard it. Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for the third time, no, until I saw this article now. And if you want one word only, then it's no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I want an answer to the question. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did Drnis ever change its name to Mladenovo or Ratkovo?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were also shown a video that I won't show again - it's P7639 - and it says that general said at the end of that clip that they could only wait for him in a destroyed city or town, meaning Drnis. Was Drnis destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to pass through Drnis several times when I was travelling for various exchanges towards Zitnic village, and I didn't see that it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Kijevo destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never passed through Kijevo village. Anything I would say would be speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know of what ethnicity the population of Kijevo is?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly Croats, whether 95 per cent or 100 per cent, I don't know, but the overwhelming majority were Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you again about Kijevo. I fully understand that the question: Was Kijevo destroyed? And you said you never saw that. Did you ever hear or read anything about the destruction of Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I didn't pass through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- that's what I -- Mr. -- Mr. Strbac --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Court is ruled by this Chamber, not by you. You know the profession. You were asked whether Kijevo was destroyed. Your answer was: I never passed through, therefore everything would be speculation. Then I put another question to you which was: Did you ever hear or read about destruction of Kijevo? There's no need to repeat your previous answer because it's a different question. I again now put that question to you: Did you ever read or hear about the destruction of Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in the sense in which you're asking. When you say "destruction," then you could think that it was destroyed 100 per cent but it could be 5 per cent. There was fighting, there were battles, and there was a certain amount of destruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could you specify? Was 25 per cent of the buildings and structures destroyed? Was it less? Was it more? Could you give us any further detail about what you read or what you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I repeat: Whether it was 5 per cent, 20 per cent, or 50 per cent, I don't know. I didn't pass through, and I don't remember reading that anywhere. All I know was that there had been battles and there was some destruction by artillery, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you suppose. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We talked yesterday about the context in which the conversation in P7639 was led, and that one was marked as 65 ter 33408d. And I would kindly ask help from Ms. Stewart to play the previous 65 ter, which is 33408c, so 33408c. And we -- there are transcripts under the same number in the e-court, so if it could be seen on the screens, at least the translators could have it, I think, on their screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, first of all, we should wait to see whether the interpreters' booths can find those transcripts. And then, second, we would have to find out whether the accuracy of that transcript was already verified; if it was, then we can play it. Interpreters' booths are ready? Yes, I see it's confirmed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I see that Ms. Stewart nodded when you asked whether it was verified, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I saw everyone was nodding in the affirmative, so I'm fully convinced. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So it's from the main video from 47 minutes 0 seconds up to 48 minutes, 15 seconds. Can we play it now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Next we will pull out all our units out of Sinj, from the Sinj garrison, and we will do that in the following order: First the equipment; the weaponry - this means all the weaponry including those from the depots except for the weapons used by the troops in the Knin garrison which you're using to defend yourself; then the equipment; the hardware; then family members of the military personnel and civilians employed in the army, and together with them, the population that does not want to stay in that area, with all their possessions. For this to be normal, we are subordinating everything to the evacuation of the families. So first, the families, then the equipment, then the weaponry, then the hardware ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, first, that the units in the Knin garrison were surrounded in the autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that, but I know - and I've spoken about it - that on the 15th of September an order had been issued for all the barracks to be blocked. Croatia issued that order and that order was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear at the time that there were attacks on family members of the JNA officers who lived in the area?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I heard that and I talked to many of them after they had crossed over to the Serbian side. I knew some of them personally because I used to work in Zadar, where there were many such officers and their families. The families were mistreated in many various ways. One of the ways was that they would be brought in front of the barracks and then forced to call out to their husbands who were inside the blocked barracks, they would call on them to surrender. They did that with children too and similar things. And this happened day-in and day-out until everything was unblocked. And, of course, some officers could not resist the temptation so they walked out or they surrendered the barracks and they joined their families. Some of them were even prosecuted later before courts in Serbia for treason.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this video into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This should then be added, and this specific excerpt has separately been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33408c receives Exhibit Number D1349, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see on our screens P07641, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was shown to you yesterday, Mr. Strbac. We will soon see it on our screens. It's also a document originating from the 9th Corps dated the 4th of October, 1991. You were shown page 2, so if we could please see the same page again so your memory would be refreshed. Under item 3, the document reads that the Chief of Staff, Colonel Ratko Mladic, said the following: "I have decided: "Continue with offensive operations towards Zadar ..." And now if we return to page 1, we see the penultimate paragraph, under item 2, it is the last paragraph in the English version. It reads: "The units took up a circular defence at favourable positions, from where they will continue the attack on Zadar in the morning in order to lift the blockade of the forces surrounded in the town." As far as you know, was this blockade continued in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in Zadar, it was. Zadar was closest. I knew many officers from Zadar, and they withdrew from Zadar via Benkovac. So of all the incidents from the early 1990s that happened during the war, this is something that was closest to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you please have a look at the transcript, page 43, line -- no, I'm -- wrong line. 43, line 2, where you are recorded as having said: "The document reads that the Chief of Staff, Colonel Ratko Mladic, said the following ..." and then "I have decided ..." First of all, I wonder, I had difficulties in finding it, apart from whether it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, let's see the last page, please. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was page 2 I think you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 2 and then we have the signature. It's wrong. I now see what you mean. In English it says "commander." In B/C/S in original it says "head of staff, Chief of Staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and apart from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it -- then it said Major General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- Vukovic. Yeah, it's up -- maybe Mladic is on the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could be, but I looked of course at paragraph 2 since you have drawn our attention to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah, now it says, yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I see it on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what he said, I don't think he said anything, but he wrote something.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he wrote something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was said that the diaries of Mr. Mladic, P349, on relevant pages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the counsel could please repeat the number of the pages in the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... number 349 and pages are from 348 up to 356.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that this is mentioned in General Mladic's diary, the operation in Skabrnja, and then 65 ter 33427 was shown, and it discusses the same events, and I will ask something with regard to Skabrnja now. Do you know when this incident in Skabrnja occurred?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th and the 19th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened then? The military convoy, did it leave?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Skabrnja was behind the Zadar airport called Zemunik, and the airport was both a military and a civilian one, and at the time it was controlled by the JNA. And very often they were threatened an occasionally Skabrnja and another village Galovac also launched attacks on it. I did not take part in this action. Later I prepared the defence for some Serbs who were accused and sentenced before Croatian courts before this operation and I learned a lot from the case files. A convoy headed by the JNA and including some TO members and some volunteers set out from Zemunik Gornji towards Skabrnja, and they were moving in a convoy down the road. It was not combat disposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second. Who was at the head of the column?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was a captain by rank and that his name was Stevanovic. He was at the head, and he held a megaphone in his hand and he called on those responsible to come out for talks and negotiations, saying that there was no need for shooting from either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. And how did he end up, this man with the megaphone?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He got a sniper shot in his forehead. The convoy stopped. Everyone found shelter behind the APCs. There were several tanks at the rear, and the convoy stood still like that for a minute or two. And then a soldier, who was serving compulsory military service and who was an ethnic Macedonian, summoned enough courage to go and see what happened with his superior because he was his ADC, inter alia, and so he got a shot in the forehead as well and he was killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this convoy what ethnicities were represented? It was a convoy pulling out from the Zemunik airport?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the convoy that was going towards Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were all ethnicities there. Still, I have mentioned that one of the casualties was a Macedonian, and I had an opportunity to read in the case file the evidence of a Croat from Makarska - I forget his last name - but he was also serving his compulsory military service at the time; and he said in one of the documents in the case file that he participated in this operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you calm down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try. You mean I should slow down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I intended to say. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mm-hmm. There were people of other ethnicities too. They reflected the ethnic composition of the then-SFRY, so there were still only a few members of the JNA who had left it during their regular service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. And did then a battle ensue?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the convoy came to their senses, if I may put it so. Someone took over the command, and they set out, and the battle lasted two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was fire opened at the convoy?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each house was armed. There were both civilians and others in the houses. The civilians were also armed and, as I was told, they had to take control of one house after another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you now put many, many questions, and we heard a lot of answers about events where, if I understand the witness well, he was not present. It's just a reconstruction of what he may have read somewhere --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or heard somewhere. I didn't stop you earlier, but you know that this is not really what we are seeking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He -- this is not only hearsay, which is also allowed in front of this Tribunal; this is his knowledge he gained through examining the documentation in preparation for the defence of some accused persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, that is a kind of hearsay; that's not forbidden in itself. That's really why I didn't stop you, but then at least the sources should be well-known --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what exactly he relied upon. I'm not -- and another matter is -- no. I leave it to that. But knowledge gained through examining the documentation is, of course, primarily what this Chamber has to do, because that implies assessments of credibility and reliability, which are not primarily for the witness to make but for this Court. That's what I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll just have a couple of more questions and I'll finish with this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll finish the topic soon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's break time. If you finish the topic soon, then perhaps we'll finish this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you just briefly tell us what were some of the sources on which you relied when you received this information?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already mentioned one source. I read the case files from the court because a group of around 16 or 17 members of the Territorial Defence from the Benkovac area stood trial before the Croatian court in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the first of the accused on the list?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Zoran Lakic, who was the commander of the Benkovac TO; I think that it was him and he was certainly among them. And now the whole case file was transferred from Croatia to Serbia on the basis of the agreement between the war crimes prosecutors of Croatia and Serbia, so I had another occasion to review the case files, and I did so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that was the case file. Any other source you consulted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked with participants who took part in the event, maybe around ten of them, with regard to the fighting itself. And as for the casualties, we already talked about it, and also the exchange connected with this; the Prosecutor asked me about that too, and I may clarify that too, if there are any questions with regard to that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you speak with participants from both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which side were those persons you spoke with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the JNA side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the case file, are there also statements of the Croatian participants?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the case file includes the statements of participants from both sides. That was where I read the statements of the young man who was a Croat from Makarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
