utterances.text: And just tell us this: Do you know anything about the status of the persons who participated in this battle on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When my commission, headed by myself, presented the mortal remains to the Croats, they did not want to take them on the first day; and then on the second day, we did hand them over. Then they were examined, and we have been shown the autopsy here ... I'm sorry, what was the question? I've lost the thread.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question about -- was about the status of the people.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. In the beginning, the Croatian side represented that they were all civilians; however, already at the first anniversary it turned out that at least 28 were members of the ZNG, the then-Croatian army, because we saw that in the notices of death in the newspapers - and the Croats later recognised it because these men were accorded the status of fighters and their families received appropriate benefits. And we also found out later that a unit was stationed there called the Independent Skabrnja Battalion; they did not have uniforms, but they did have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were they put up in Benkovac when people from Skabrnja were brought?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people were escorted, saved from their houses. Some elderly people, women and children, and they brought them to Benkovac and placed them in the building of a kindergarten, where there were no children but there were Serbian families that had been brought a couple of days before from some peripheral Serbian villages where there had been a lot of combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From which area were these Serbs that were in the same kindergarten?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The greatest number was from a village called Lisane Tinjske which was close to Skabrnja and Galovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be all on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have passed the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you give us an indication as to how much time you'd still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I should finish in 15 minutes 10, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten, 15 minutes, yes. When I earlier -- when I gave some comments on hearsay, et cetera, of course, this is more or less even expert testimony, evaluating whatever the sources tell you. If Mr. Riedlmayer does the same, then he is an expert and this witness tells us exactly what happens. The sources are generally known but not in any detail -- they're certainly not available to the Chamber. I would like you to keep that in mind for after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We can provide the Chamber probably with that file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll see what you do and what the Prosecution's response that will be. We take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the witness -- oh, I'm sorry to interrupt. Before the witness is with us, I can say that in regard of 65 ter 33410, we would like to add two previous pages. So only page 115 was offered. We would ask kindly to have 114 and 113, and it would correspond to the transcript numbers 12548 and 12549.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And that was already admitted as P7645?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now the request is understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was -- I think I more or less even invited you to tell us whether you wanted more. May I take that a new version which will then replace the present P7645 will be prepared and uploaded so that we can instruct Madam Registrar to replace the current version by the new version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Strbac, I will have to torment you for another 10, 15 minutes. We saw that example when you participated in the first exchange as a lawyer, when there were five arrested Serbs and eight arrested Croats. Apart from that example, do you know whether the Serbian side rounded up civilians in the street in order to send them for an exchange?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've explained that; I explained it on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. But at one moment you said both sides held civilians. From where did these civilians come?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Serbian side, they were arrested for some criminal offences, and at some point they would be sent for an exchange because the other side was seeking them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek clarification. You said "on the Serbian side." Are we -- I asked you questions about the five Serbs and the eight Croats. If you say "on the Serbian side, they were arrested," do you refer to the Croats, Croats being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For the most part, Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, earlier I asked you why there were arrested. You now say they were arrested for some criminal offences. Earlier you said, as far as you knew, they were arrested just for the purpose of being exchanged, and you had no idea about -- for what reasons, that would be speculation. And now you are telling us that they were arrested for offences, some criminal offences --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- the first question was for those eight. And my question now was in general, not for those eight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I said specifically beside these eight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then why would you not know about the eight and why would you know about the others, for the reasons of their arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say explicitly that I didn't know. All the time I've been answering that I did not see the papers, the file. I saw -- I mean, that was one special case. Now a general question was asked about something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ... Yes. Mr. Lukic, I was -- when you said -- you said both sides held civilians, from where did these civilians come. This was not as clearly separated as in your previous question, where you indeed made a distinction and where the witness said that he had explained it already and -- and that was perhaps not that clearly explained --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it is still unclear whether it was the eight and the five or whether it's a more general question. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have on our screens P7647, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was shown to you, Mr. Strbac - and we'll see it on our screens soon - a text from domestic newspapers translated into English, but we can't see who the authors of the text are, so I can't ask you specifically -- because you can't see the author of that text, I can't ask you if you really gave that interview.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be France Presse.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's no signature at the end, but we see at the top that Viktorija Stegic is referenced. Did you give an interview to this lady?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember such a lady, but if I see correctly it should be the Agence France Presse.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the agency published this story, but --

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that lady, but I don't rule out the possibility. I gave interviews to hundreds of newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I would like to see briefly P7648. It is said that this is an interview given by President Milosevic; in fact, his speech at an Extraordinary Session of the Assembly of Serbia. The date is 9 August 1991. It's the penultimate paragraph in the B/C/S and third from the bottom in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I see the date of 29th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: English. But on the other side it's 9 August, so it's probably different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is one and the same if you see in B/C/S up that says the British Broadcasting Corporation, BBC, 29th of February, 1992. And then there is a date in B/C/S underneath, Friday, August the 9th, 1991, what we do not see in English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it may be a transcription or a translation error. It's not that much of a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The English is the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the B/C/S version should be reviewed. You take proper action for that, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us focus on this paragraph. We'll see later what is the source is, whether the English version or the B/C/S. You remarked correctly when my colleague Mr. Zec was examining you. It says here, I quote: "The Republic of Serbia helped the Serbian people in this area first materially in money, food, clothing, medicines; then politically ..." And it goes on to say: "... and when all this was not enough, with arms too ... first of all, through firm support and commitment by Serbia towards the Yugoslav People's Army ..." Now I'm not sure how to ask you this, because I'm not sure whether the text is from August 1991 or February 1992. You've told us that there were volunteers present. Did you -- in fact, in the area of the Serbian Autonomous Republic Krajina, were there any military depots on the ground already when the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time when we had a common state, there were depots. Every larger military unit had its own depot. There were depots belonging to corps and smaller units. I know that close to Benkovac, where I lived, was one depot; such places were very well secured, defended, dug into the ground. Then during the war, nobody left these depots completely empty of weapons. I mentioned yesterday that Tepic nearby Bjelovar blew up one such depot with 100 tonnes of explosive, and he said it was just a small quantity of all the explosives that were in that depot. But regardless of the date of this, even if it's February 1992, it speaks of something that happened in the past. I have to tell you that the JNA officially withdrew from the territory of Croatia, including the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina where it had the most units, on 19 May 1991. That's when it pulled out, both out of Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And just one more question to conclude. Did you know in which way the units of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina were being armed?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some things I knew; others I didn't know. As for the part that I was aware of - since I was a member of the Territorial Defence like most people, regardless of ethnicity - it was that concept of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Tito's Yugoslavia, that nothing must surprise us. Most people were armed. Some had weapons at home, that was the reserve police, the Territorial Defence. Sometimes they left their weapons in depots; sometimes they took weapons home. That's how both sides got armed. Now what other sources of arming existed, we can discuss that. Croats purchased abroad. We've already discussed how many weapons they imported from Hungary. Weapons were brought by air-lift. One such air-lift was seized at the Zagreb airport. And the Serbs also had their own channels for arming. There was the JNA which sided with the Serbs and was present there until 19 May 1991. Following the logic of things - and the Territorial Defence was part of the armed forces - they were a side, a party to the conflict. So some of the weapons came from the JNA, from the depots that already existed on the grouped.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, thank you. That is all we had for you.

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've one question for you in relation to your last answer. You give a picture where weaponry that was there in depots, that that remained there, and that was more or less the explanation for what Mr. Milosevic had said. You also said something about volunteers, but I take it volunteers were not ready available in depots and were just sent from Serbia, as the document reads, to Croatia. That seems to be a bit -- a different picture from the weaponry picture. Do you have any comment on this observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean volunteers? If somebody is a volunteer, that means he is not sent by the state. In the theatres of war, in Croatia, in Bosnia, there were Dutch people, Ukrainians, Russians, there were Serbs from Serbia. As well, people organised themselves and went there. I don't know what Milosevic meant when he said "volunteers."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you're saying volunteers are not sent by governments. At the same time this document says large number of volunteers that Serbia sent to the front in Croatia, which suggests otherwise. Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you, I don't know what Milosevic meant by that. I told you what I knew. If a person is a volunteer, that means he is coming voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, any questions in --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: One short issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, today you were asked about various places in Krajina, about military operations around these places, and you have provided a lot of details about combat, about shootings. Now the fact is that crimes against Croats were taking place across the area. These crimes were known and you know that these crimes against Croats were committed; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What am I supposed to answer to a question like this? If I told you that I turned over 40-plus bodies from Skabrnja and that all these people got killed in a fierce battle, how can I now say whether it's a war crime? I don't know. It was a battle. There was fighting, fierce fighting, in Kijevo and everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... provide example, Skabrnja, Kijevo, but this was taking place across the area, that was known that these crimes were taking place; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One -- one second. I think it was asked, not answered. Please proceed. Complete your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these events, incidents, that we are discussing, it's not that somebody came and killed people while they were sleeping. There were battles that lasted day or two. People got killed. There was fighting, door-to-door fighting in populated areas. When something like that crosses the line and becomes a war crime, that's something that courts eventually decide and courts have been engaged with this for 20-plus years, including your court. In the case of Skabrnja, ten or more people went on trial. I mentioned one judgement including 16 accused. I cannot answer a question like this, whether there were crimes. There was fighting, there were casualties, but what is a crime? I don't know. All these courts would not be necessary if I were able to answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, you're not saying that all these civilian casualties were just -- just combat casualties, that you allow for the possibility that some of them or -- were the result of criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Yes, and it was so on both sides, unfortunately. There were all kinds of units or individuals who killed, looted. There was fighting against them too. It was more successful or less successful, and it happened on the Croatian side as well as the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If I -- if I may, just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Strbac, I refer what you said during your testimony in the Hadzic case. You were specifically asked about an article that you provided in your interview and you said -- the question was: "Crimes against Croats were no secret in the first place. The cases of suffering of Croats across the area of Knin were being followed by international teams ..." And you said: "I stated something like this many, many times, so I suppose I said it to them as well." So this is your testimony in Hadzic and you stand by this testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO STRBAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when it's taken out of context like this, it really sounds somehow too stark. Whatever I say, it seems to me that something will still remain unsaid and I'm not a man who likes to give answers that are incomplete. I like all of that to have and make some sense, so let me repeat. Everything that happened to the Croats, each single murder or any other crime that happened in the war, was it investigated? I would say yes, up to 99 per cent. 1755 members of the JNA and other Serbs were -- have been sentenced in front of Croatian courts, and those who were accused were more than 3 and a half thousand in numbers. But, on the other hand, the crimes against the Serbs remain uninvestigated. That was my main thought, which -- my main thesis which I presented then and which I still stand by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question, but I think we leave it to that, Mr. Zec. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes. I would only suggest that this one page that I read in the transcript page from the Hadzic case to be attached to that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it is -- if it is a literal quote, then there's no need. If it's contested that this is a quote from the Hadzic case --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, we probably have to have more because of the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I suggest the following: That you discuss with Mr. Lukic what portion you'd like to have in evidence and I don't think then that we need the witness to remain for that purpose. So we'll hear from the parties together what excerpts are selected. Mr. Strbac, this concludes your evidence in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague. You've answered questions put to you by the parties, by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. And you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It was my pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is your next witness, who is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't know if he is ready. We don't have any kind of contact with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I see that, but -- I shouldn't have addressed you, Mr. Lukic. Is the next witness ready to enter the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we're at a point where the next witness, that the cross-examination will continue, Mr. Traldi, isn't it? And that would be Mr. Kijac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We'll just take a moment to organise ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber never opposes a party organising itself, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kijac. Mr. Kijac, we'll now continue. You have returned home and are now back. And you'll remember that you were about -- you were being cross-examined by Mr. Traldi when the session was interrupted. I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, although that's a couple of weeks ago. Mr. Traldi will now continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit D1300 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 46 of your statement, you refer to orders you and President Karadzic issued which you characterise as directing that crimes in Republika Srpska be investigated, especially in Prijedor. This is the Karadzic order you mention. We see it's dated 3 April 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32749.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, you and President Karadzic, of course, both knew that serious crimes had been committed against Bosnian Muslims and Croats in Prijedor municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please just return the president's order to the screen so I might read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'd directed your attention to the point that I'd been interested in. I'd ask you to answer my question. You and President Karadzic both knew that serious crimes had been committed against Bosnian Muslims and Croats in Prijedor municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have found me in a state where I'm not really ready. I would like to see the president's orders again. And as for the crimes in Prijedor, I would like to make it clear that we as a service did not have such information. As the State Security Service, we did not investigate war crimes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm asking you as a human being, did you know, yes or no, that serious crimes had been committed against Bosnian Muslims and Croats in Prijedor? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such stories; however, the state security department was not informed along its line of information about the events in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a summary of a conversation intercepted by the Croatian authorities in late May of 1992. We read that people they referred to as "the enemy are killing prisoners who had weapons east of Prijedor around Kozarac." Now first, at this point we agree, I take it, that the Croatian forces' enemy was the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. To what says in the document, this is intercept of -- the intercept should say what's said. If the intercept says that enemy, then enemy should be somebody who is Serb's enemy. If it's somebody on the Serbian side who is speaking, so giving the interpretation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- Mr. Lukic, this is not an objection. Yes, first of all, if Mr. Traldi puts a leading question, he is allowed to do so in cross-examination. Mr. Traldi explained to the witness what this was, and this apparently is a non-verbal -- transcribed telephone intercept -- or communications interception. That's how it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I want to see where in the document it is said what Mr. Traldi is claiming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, There's no need. You can re-visit the matter in re-examination, if there's any need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I want reference, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- I want reference from the document where this claim is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that's all I ask for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear that you want that, and I gave an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think Mr. Traldi read this intercept and then asked a question separate from the intercept to say: Can you and I agree that "enemy" here means a Serb? He is not claiming that that's what's contained here. He's asking the witness if he would agree that the "enemy" refers to a -- to the Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On which base? That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is just a question. Does it have to have a basis? He is just asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thinking on the basis of intercept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have tried to explain what I thought the question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I take it that you started from the assumption that it was a Serb who is recorded here as speaking and that, in that context, you are asking about who would be an enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the basis that I'd put and in future it would be better to have a detailed discussion of the basis like this outside the presence of the witness, but since we've done most of it, the basis for my question was the summary is prepared by the Croatian authorities, is descriptive, comes from a collection of intercepts, including other summaries prepared by the Croatian authorities and refers to the enemy. What I'd asked the witness was: Can we agree late May 1992 the Croatian forces' enemy in Prijedor was the VRS? And I think it's a completely fair question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- well, Mr. Lukic, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just follow on your question, Your Honour. It's not answered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to that, Mr. Lukic. You have to accept that. If there are any further questions to be asked about this, you can do that in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is my ruling at this moment and all questions you still may have you can raise them in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have an objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that objection is overruled and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another one. What's your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is base for the claim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an objection; that's a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- that Serbs are intercepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a question, Mr. Lukic. Where is your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My objection is that this is misrepresentation of the evidence. There is no basis for claim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That objection is also denied. Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the witness should answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll try one more time, sir, can we agree that the Croatian forces' enemy and the Bosnian Croat forces' enemy in Prijedor municipality in late May 1992 was the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we read here the enemy is killing prisoners. You knew that prisoners held by the VRS and other Bosnian Serb forces were held in criminal conditions in Prijedor municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this. In May 1992, I was the centre chief in Sarajevo together with other regional centres I did not have any connection with them. And I had no information about Prijedor whatsoever. So this had to do with the then-head of service. I don't know whether he knew that. Those of us in Sarajevo had nothing to do with Prijedor because I was not in charge of Prijedor at the time but, rather, in charge of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P6659.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And 6659, as it comes up, sir, I'd ask you to focus on my question rather than re-explaining the structure of the RS MUP. Now this is a summary of a meeting of a MUP senior officials on the 11th of July 1992. Turning to page 2 in both languages, we see in the second paragraph a list of attendees. And just a couple of lines up from the bottom of the second paragraph, we see references to Zoran Cvijetic, chief of the centre, and Dragan Kijac, chief of the SNB sector. Now Dragan Kijac refers to you; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone because we can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you come closer to the microphone and speak into it and repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, probably yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 7 in both languages, we'll see a part of Stojan Zupljanin's remarks. Now he was the head of CSB Banja Luka and had responsibility for the region of the Bosnian Krajina, including Prijedor, and the RS MUP side; right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me not read all this, but I can confirm that Mr. Zupljanin was responsible for the area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the microphone of the witness be adjusted more or less to his -- because if you are leaning in that direction, then the microphone should be in that direction as well. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now he says at the first bullet point: "The army and Crisis Staffs, or War Presidencies, are requesting that as many Muslims as possible are gathered, and they are leaving these undefined camps up to the internal affairs organs. Conditions in these camps are bad - there is no food, some individuals do not observe international norms because, among other things, such collection centres are not adequate or there are other reasons ..." So first, at this meeting where we saw you on the list of attendees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, are you sure that we are on the right page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll double-check, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I can't see it anymore --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We should turn to the next page in B/C/S and it will at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We can now see the first hyphen starts with [B/C/S spoken]. Sir, I'll ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At this meeting where we saw you on the list of attendees, you would have learned no later than the 11th of July, 1992, that Muslims were being gathered and left in camps with no food and in places where international norms weren't being observed; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether these were camps or collection centres because I didn't go there. It was a regular meeting at which the State Security Service probably did not -- usually did not take part in discussion. We had nothing to do with these issues. We were not in charge of camps. We were not --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir, I understand you're trying to focus on your own relationship with these camps. What I'm asking you is: Setting aside your professional responsibility, as a human being on 11 July 1992, when Zupljanin said this, you knew Muslims were being gathered and left in camps with no food, where international norms weren't being observed; you knew that then, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, that there were collection centres and everything else simply did not reach me and I wasn't interested in it because I was not responsible for it and it was not the domain for which I was in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I then understand that you heard half of the sentence and not the remainder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't even remember this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember this. It was a long time ago, but I accept that it was so. I cannot say that it wasn't so. If these are the minutes and this is the report, I accept it as such. I'm just telling from my own point of view and from the point of view of the remit of the work of my service. The service had nothing to do with such persons. There was simply so much information that some of it slipped by unnoticed by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may have missed that information. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 02653.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a document sent by and signed for the chief of the SNB sector in Banja Luka, Nedjelko Kesic, dated 12th of June, 1992, requesting that three persons, Anto Mandic, Nedeljko Maric, and Miro Petrusic, be released to undergo further investigation at the Banja Luka CSB. Now, this is a reflection that the national security sector had a role in processing prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, this has nothing to do with Prijedor. This is the Banja Luka district prison. So even the last time I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... simply answer the question I asked you. This reflects that the national security sector had a role in processing prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: State security, once again, you are pointing to something when I wasn't in charge of the service, but I will answer you in general terms. The state security did show interest in certain prisoners and worked with them. It's not in dispute. I said that last time. When it was in the interests of the service to work with someone or to process certain individuals - as we professionally would put it - then there's no dispute that the centre, the Security Services Centre from Banja Luka, probably requested these three persons in order to interview them and then probably sent them back to the Banja Luka district prison upon completing the operative processing of these persons. We did that. I'm not aware of this particular incident, but generally did that with prisoners of war who were of interest for our service. And if you like, I may clarify to you what the interests of the service may stand for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: One of the places that there were National Security Service officials doing that was Omarska camp, right, in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you certainly knew from -- sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, don't interrupt. You've answered the question. Mr. Traldi was about to phrase a new question for you. Don't interrupt him, please. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you certainly knew, like everyone else who could read a newspaper and see a television, you knew long before April 2004 that that would -- or sorry, April 1994 that Omarska camp was one of the places where serious crimes had been committed against non-Serbs in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We don't have a single paper that came from the security service Banja Luka informing us of that situation. Find me one single paper where the centre Banja Luka informs the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm stopping you there again because you have not carefully listened to the question - because it was not whether you received any official documents about that - but you were asked whether you knew and it was referred to "like everyone else who could read a newspaper and see a television," so apparently not the formal sources were hinted at by Mr. Traldi but, rather, sources available to everyone. Knowledge is the question, not whether you received it officially. Could you please answer the question, whether you knew before 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I knew what the television reported when foreign reporters came to the area of Prijedor, to those collection centres. I don't remember which month it was, but I remember there were a couple of movies on TV about access given to foreign reporters to these centres in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But those crimes weren't the subject of the orders you and Mr. Karadzic issued; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which crimes you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Would it refresh your recollection if I put to you that there'd been a small number of murders in Prijedor municipality in late March 1994, just before your order and President Karadzic's order were issued, and that the Red Cross had threatened to evacuate every remaining Muslim and Croat from Prijedor as a result?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let's get one thing clear. Mr. Karadzic and I could not give orders. The president could give an order, and I could only convey it. I could not give orders to them, structures which do not belong to the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, your question contains several elements. I think you would be more successful in getting answers if you split them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll try and take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You say in your statement that President Karadzic issued an order - April 3rd, 1994 - that you conveyed to your subordinates. We saw that order a moment ago. Would it refresh your recollection that what that was ordering an investigation of was a small number of murders in late March 1994, not any of the crimes in the camps or the cleansing in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I get my written statement, please, because I don't have it before me. I want to see how I formulated it in the statements. And second, you know that the State Security Service does not investigate war crimes. That was defined in 1992 within the Ministry of the Interior when, according to the distribution of certain --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of certain powers and jurisdictions --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Again, you've moved on to repeating evidence about the structure of the MUP that you've given a number of times. I'd encourage you, please, to focus on the questions you're asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When that order was shown to this gentleman, he asked to see it again so he didn't see it properly. Now he is asking for his statement, and nothing has been shown. And it -- still my learned friend is insisting on his answer. So I don't think that -- this is proper way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether it is proper or not, I just -- Mr. -- would have you any problem with providing the witness with his statement, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it would be inappropriate to ask a question about a statement without giving the witness that statement is a matter different from what we do now, that is, that the witness will be given his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but the order D130 -- what was the number? D1300. He asked kindly to see that order, because obviously he didn't see it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if he --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now he is asked about the same order again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If he gave a statement about an order, then not under all circumstances it's inappropriate to put a question without showing that document again. At the same time, Mr. Traldi, if that is not part of your strategy, then I think it would be better to meet such a request from our witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I certainly don't have any reason not call it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have D1300, and I have a clean copy of the B/C/S -- or what I'm told is a clean copy of the B/C/S, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you is: This order referred to crimes committed in late March 1994. That's what it was about; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does not say when the crimes were committed. It says: "Take all the steps to investigate crimes committed in Republika Srpska, in particularly Prijedor." I don't see which period it relates to, but let us accept that it was in 1994. You are probably looking at the date of the order. It's 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll take a break and we will resume at five minutes to 2.00, but first the witness may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile, Mr. Traldi, I started interpreting your question on page 66, line 11; I think I didn't do that well and I'd better refrain of doing it. It may have confused rather than contribute anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I admit I had forgotten it entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Before I forget anything else, three of the documents that you used last session I'd seek to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you certainly will have the 65 ter numbers ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the first one I'd tender is 02653. That's the SNB Banja Luka request about the three detained persons.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives Exhibit Number P7650.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And then under seal the last two documents I used, 23768 and 23770.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And those would receive, Madam Registrar, numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 23768 receives Exhibit Number P7651. 65 ter number 23770 receives Exhibit Number P7652, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7651 and P7652 are admitted into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And could we please have P7650 on the screen because I would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge has a question for you, Mr. Kijac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kijac, you have seen this document before the break. I refer you to one of your previous answers on page 72, lines 7 to 11. You said, among other things: "... there's no dispute that the centre, the Security Services Centre from Banja Luka, probably requested these three persons in order to interview them and then probably sent them back to the Banja Luka district prison upon completing the operative processing of these persons." If you now look at the last sentence of this document before you, it reads: "You are holding the above-named in accordance with our decisions," and then three numbers are following, "... of 11 June 1992." What does -- can you comment on that? Can you explain what that means "in accordance with our decisions"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Your Honour, I noticed this. I would just like to say that we are talking about assumptions only, considering that in this period I was not the chief of this service. But I suppose that complaints had been filed against these persons and that they were detained because of that, and they were in remand. So when it says "our decisions," I suppose that these were decisions of the state security, according to which they were placed in remand. And I suppose the corresponding criminal complaints had been filed with the appropriate court or the prosecutor's office. They must have had certain information on which they based these decisions to place them in remand. I don't know about this specific case, but according to the logic of our service, if somebody had been placed in an investigative prison, that there must be some suspicion that the person had done something; or perhaps the prosecutor's office was not happy with such a decision and wanted to interview them additionally. This is the regular procedure. We're talking about standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand that you were talking -- or conveying your assumptions to me. But what does it mean? Can I take it from this document that these people were detained by the SNB sector?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, he says CSB Security Service Centre Banja Luka. I supposed that it could be the State Security Sector, and it's signed by the state sector chief, Mr. Kesic, saying above "our decisions." Therefore, I suppose that the decision to place them in remand was taken by the sector of the state security Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps just a short follow-up question. From your previous answer I gained the impression - right or wrong - that the service was just borrowing them. You are detaining them, we'd like to interview them, whereas, on the basis of the question Judge Fluegge did put to you, it seems that it was under the responsibility of the Security Services Centre Banja Luka that they were detained, not that they would borrow them but they were the ones who had ordered the detention. Is that now well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly -- again, I'm guessing only. Maybe some other people through surveillance found out that they were involved in hostile activity and they were therefore detained and criminal complaints were filed against them, but I'm supposing only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's different from my question. But I think having re-read your previous answer, I think my question may have been superfluous. Mr. Traldi, you may proceed. At the same time, I'm drawing your attention to the following, that -- could you consider and check whether P7651 and 7652 really should be under seal as I said. Could you please verify that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, my colleagues have informed me that there are good reasons for that. So therefore I should perhaps have a bit more trust in your assessment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll try to deserve that, Your Honour. Could we have 65 ter 09406.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a United Nations telegram dated the 1st of April, 1994. We see in the second paragraph. And in the first paragraph we see a reference to "first nine dead" and then "now 22." The second paragraph we see the Red Cross will therefore advise Karadzic that they will evacuate all of 6.000 Muslim population Prijedor who may wish to leave and also 3.000 Croats. Now when you were here three weeks ago, we agreed that Mr. Zupljanin had been proposing to offer contracts to some non-Serbs in the RS MUP for PR reason, for public relations reasons. The impact of evacuating the few remaining non-Serbs from Prijedor on the Republika Srpska's international image would have been very negative; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Traldi, but I don't have a translation of this document. I can only see an English version, so if you could please provide me with a translation so I could see for myself what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise, sir, we don't have one yet. Does a translation or does the lack of a translation make you unable to answer my question as to whether the evacuation of the few remaining Muslims and Croats from Prijedor would have had a negative effect on the Republika Srpska's international image?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would object to this point. I don't know if 9.000 could be called few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, would you please read the second paragraph to the witness and then ask your question again, because the question was put in relation to a document the witness is unable to read. So if would you read that and slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Paragraph begins: "ICRC will therefore advise Karadzic that they will evacuate all of 6.000 Muslim population Prijedor who may wish to leave, also 3.000 Croats. Assumption is that it is safer now to evacuate" -- it says "there persons than for them to stay."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you agree that this evacuation would have had a very negative effect on the Republika Srpska's international image if it had been carried out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hardly answer that question for the simple reason that I have not been following this case. That's one. And another thing is that you have to have in mind that some of the non-Serb population from certain areas requested to leave the territory of Republika Srpska. As far as I know, in Prijedor, there were some non-Serbs who were serving in the Army of Republika Srpska. I don't know the figures, but I suppose you have those.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how is it that you are unable to comment on discussions of camps in Prijedor that occurred at meetings you attended but you are able to offer information about the ethnic composition of VRS units in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because by watching these testimonies, I saw some witnesses who offered some information --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and secondly, I can hardly --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: By "these testimonies," you mean testimonies in this trial?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at trials. I don't know if this was this one or some other trials --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for the remainder of your testimony if the information are you providing is based on something you heard from a different witness at this Court years after years after the war, can we agree that it would be best if you made that clear during the course of your answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I indicated that in connection with this last question of yours, on the one hand; and on the other hand, Mr. Traldi, I am not the one who is to say what could damage Republika Srpska. I was a high-ranking official who was in charge of intelligence rather than someone who assessed politics and what politicians wanted to achieve at any given moment. You have to admit that however high a position I held in the intelligence circles, I was not involved in politics. I was not a member of the government or of the parliament or even a member of the party, so I did not really engage in politics but I was doing professional work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 31513.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I put one question awaiting that document to appear on our screens. You said: "I am not the one who is to say what could damage Republika Srpska ..." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Traldi asked me how the international public would react to such a move. That was how I understood him, that this was the essential issue, how the international public would react to the evacuation of such a number of non-Serbs from the area of Prijedor. And as an official, as someone who was an employee, was not someone who could decide that. It was up to the politics to decide that. My service did not deal with such issues. We did not follow convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the proper answer would have been: I never developed any thoughts on that; or, if you have developed any thoughts on that, then to say what those thoughts were. Mr. Traldi, at the same time, you are asking for opinion rather than for facts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a decree signed by President Karadzic dated 17 November 1995 decorating many of the members of the RS MUP. Turning to page 4 in both languages, under Petar Mrkonjic Medal, we see at number 6 the public security centre in Prijedor. Now this is an endorsement of that centre's work; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under number 6, it's the public security centre, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Page 8 in the English, 7 in the B/C/S, number 90, and we'll be in a category called Merit for the People Medal, we see Ranko Mijic from CJB [sic] Prijedor. He headed the SJB Prijedor interrogators at Omarska. This is also an endorsement of his work, right, giving him this award?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, when we talk about awards, each centre proposed that some of its employees be awarded. This is collected by the minister of the interior, who then forwards such information to the president of the republic. So not everyone who was proposed from the regional centre really received the award. The proposal comes from the base, so to speak; it is received by the administrations of the MUP who are in charge; they then give their final opinion; and then the proposal is submitted to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, just two more examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we can have page 14 in English, 13 in B/C/S, number 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As we turn to that I can tell that you is the decree from the president; it's not one of the proposals. Now under Military Credit Medal, 21, we see Miroslav Kvocka from CJB Prijedor. You mentioned you followed some trials here. Did you happen to notice that he was convicted of crime against humanity at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard about Kvocka. But I tell you once again that the proposal was sent from the base, and I who dealt with the Ministry of the Interior, if you presented this list to me, I would tell you that I am not familiar with 90 per cent of these people. And can you imagine what happened when the president of the republic received this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going ask you about one more name that you might be familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we can turn back to page 1 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that should be your last question from today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see under Star of Karadjordje Battle 2nd Class Ljubomir Borovcanin from Special Police Brigade, he has also been convicted at the Tribunal in his case for crimes committed at Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 09406 -- sorry, that one I asked to have MFI'd pending a translation. And I tender this document, 65 ter 31513.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the first one without translation?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 09406 receives Exhibit Number P7653.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 31513 receives Exhibit Number P7654.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. We'll adjourn for the day, Mr. Kijac. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. I would -- I instruct you that you shouldn't speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. If that's clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 12th of November, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of November, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.21 p.m.,
